math constants: math.pi ≈ 3.141592653589793, math.e ≈ 2.718281828459045. Functions: sqrt(x) (float), ceil(x) (smallest integer ≥ x), floor(x) (largest integer ≤ x), fabs(x) (absolute value as float), sin(x), cos(x), tan(x) (x in radians).
Also: factorial(n) (n!), gcd(a, b) (HCF), fmod(x, y) (float remainder, sign of x: fmod(−7, 3) = −1.0, while −7 % 3 = 2).
Built-in pow(2, 3) gives 8 (int for int arguments); math.pow(2, 3) always gives a float, 8.0.

ex.q: Evaluate math.ceil(4.2), math.floor(−4.2), math.sqrt(49), math.factorial(4), math.gcd(12, 18).

topics.rl: ISRO trajectory calculations use the same math functions (sin, cos, sqrt) that you can import in one line.

topics.h: A Ludo app 'rolls' a die with random.randint(1, 6). Every board game app you've played leans on the random module.
p: random.random() returns a float x with 0.0 ≤ x < 1.0 (never 1.0).
random.randint(a, b) returns an integer N with a ≤ N ≤ b; BOTH ends are included.
random.randrange(start, stop, step) returns a random element of range(start, stop, step); stop is NOT included. randrange(10) gives 0 to 9.

statistics.mean(data) is the average; statistics.median(data) is the middle value of the sorted data (average of the two middle values for an even count); statistics.mode(data) is the most frequent value.
Exam tasks: predict outputs of tuple/dictionary code, find the possible outputs of random code, and write programs using dictionaries and modules.

ex.q: For data = [2, 7, 4, 7, 5], find mean, median and mode.

topics.rl: Lottery-style draws, OTP generation demos and 'shuffle' in music apps all rely on random numbers, while statistics.mean() and median() summarise exam results.

topics.h: That embarrassing comment from Class 8 could show up when a college or employer searches your name. The internet has a long memory.
p: Digital technology makes banking, learning and communication faster and easier, but the same tools can be misused, so we must use them responsibly.
A digital footprint is the trail of data you leave behind while using the internet: posts, searches, sites visited, purchases, location and more.
Active digital footprint: data you share intentionally, such as posts, comments, emails, uploaded photos and online forms you fill.
Passive digital footprint: data collected without you actively sharing it, such as browsing history, cookies, IP address, app usage and location tracking.

Footprints are stored on your device (browser history, cookies) and on remote servers of websites and apps. Even after you delete a post, copies may remain, so footprints are very hard to erase completely.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a reel you posted, (b) a shopping site remembering what you viewed, (c) a review you wrote, (d) your phone's location history.
st: (b) Recorded through cookies while browsing → passive
ex.a: Active: a, c. Passive: b, d.

topics.rl: Recruiters and college admission teams sometimes look at applicants' public social media. A thoughtful online presence can open doors; a careless one can close them.

topics.h: In a group chat of 200 classmates, one rude forward can ruin everyone's day. Being a good netizen is about small, everyday choices.
p: A digital society uses digital technology in every part of life. A netizen (internet + citizen) is anyone who uses the internet; a responsible netizen follows safe, ethical and legal practices.

Net etiquette: Be ethical (don't violate copyright; share your expertise), be respectful (respect privacy and diversity of opinions, cultures and backgrounds), be responsible (avoid cyberbullying; don't feed the trolls, i.e. ignore provocative posts).

Communication etiquette (email, chat, comments): be precise (respect others' time and data limits; don't send huge unnecessary files), be polite, and be credible (think before you comment). Avoid spam and mass forwards.
Social media etiquette: be secure (strong passwords, know who you befriend, beware of fake news and fake profiles) and be reliable (think before uploading: posts and photos may stay online for ever).

ex.q: Classify each: (a) ignoring a troll's insulting comment, (b) forwarding unverified news, (c) crediting a photographer when sharing their picture, (d) accepting requests from unknown profiles.
st: (a) Don't feed the trolls → good (be responsible)
(b) Spreading possible fake news → bad (be secure/reliable)
(c) Respecting the creator's rights → good (be ethical)
(d) Not knowing who you befriend → bad (be secure)
ex.a: Good: a, c. Bad: b, d.

topics.rl: During exam results season, fake 'CBSE result links' spread on WhatsApp. A responsible netizen checks the official website before forwarding anything.

topics.t: Data protection, intellectual property and licences
topics.h: The song you're humming, the logo on your shoes and the medicine your grandmother takes are all protected by intellectual property laws.
p: Data protection keeps sensitive personal data (bank details, health records, passwords, Aadhaar) safe through encryption, authentication (passwords, OTPs, biometrics) and data-protection laws.

Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) protect creations of the mind. Copyright protects creative and literary work (books, music, software code, films). A patent protects an invention, usually for about 20 years. A trademark protects a brand's name, logo or symbol.

Violations: plagiarism (presenting someone else's work as your own without credit), copyright infringement (using protected work without permission), trademark infringement (using another's mark without permission).

Public-access licences let creators share work: Creative Commons (CC) for creative content; GNU GPL and Apache for software. FOSS (Free and Open Source Software) lets users use, study, modify and share code.
Software piracy is the unauthorised copying, distribution or use of software, and is illegal.

ex.q: Classify: (a) copying a blog post into your project without credit, (b) a startup using a logo almost identical to a famous brand's, (c) selling copied DVDs of a new film.
st: (a) Using another's words as your own → plagiarism
(b) Misusing a brand's mark → trademark infringement
(c) Distributing protected work without permission → copyright infringement (piracy)

topics.rl: Indian generic drug makers can produce a medicine once its patent expires. Meanwhile, Bollywood producers fight film piracy because every pirated copy is lost revenue.

topics.t: Cyber crime: hacking, phishing, ransomware and bullying
topics.h: 'Your KYC has expired. Click here to update or your account will be blocked.' Thousands of Indians lose money to messages like this every year.
p: Cyber crime is any criminal activity in which a computer or network is used as a tool, a target, or both.

Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system. Ethical (white hat) hackers are authorised to find security weaknesses so they can be fixed; non-ethical (black hat) hackers break in to steal, damage or demand money.

Phishing: fake emails, SMSes or websites that look genuine trick people into revealing passwords, OTPs or card details. Email spoofing fakes the sender's address. Identity theft uses stolen personal details for fraud: financial (bank fraud), criminal (committing crimes in another's name) or medical (claiming treatment).
Ransomware encrypts the victim's files and demands payment (ransom) to unlock them. It spreads through malicious email attachments, fake downloads and infected websites or networks.
Eavesdropping: secretly intercepting communication on a network. Cyber trolls post provocative comments to upset people. Cyberbullying is using digital media to harass, threaten or humiliate someone.

ex.q: A student gets an email from 'support@paypa1-secure.com' asking for an OTP to 'stop a payment'. Identify the crime and the red flags.
st: The sender's address is a fake look-alike ('paypa1' uses the digit 1 in place of 'l'), made to pass as a trusted sender (spoofing)
It asks for an OTP, which no genuine company ever asks for
This is phishing aimed at financial identity theft

topics.rl: The 2017 WannaCry ransomware attack hit systems in many countries, including India. And the national cyber-crime helpline 1930 receives calls daily about UPI and KYC phishing scams.

topics.t: Cyber safety, malware and preventing cyber crime
topics.h: A free 'game hack' app asks for access to your SMS and contacts. That's not a game; that could be a trojan.
p: Cyber safety means using the internet safely: browsing only trusted (HTTPS) sites, protecting your identity (not over-sharing personal details), and keeping information confidential (never sharing passwords or OTPs).

Malware (malicious software) types: a virus attaches itself to files or programs and spreads when they are run; a worm copies itself across networks on its own; a trojan pretends to be useful software but harms the system; spyware secretly collects your information; adware shows unwanted advertisements.

Prevention: take regular backups; use and update antivirus software; keep the OS and apps updated; use strong, different passwords and two-factor authentication; check for HTTPS and the padlock icon; don't open unknown attachments or links.
Digital signatures verify that a document or email really comes from the claimed sender and hasn't been altered.
Report cyber crime to the local cyber cell, the national portal cybercrime.gov.in, or the helpline 1930 for financial frauds.

ex.q: Make a strong password from the idea 'I love cricket since 2015'.
st: Use initials, numbers, symbols and mixed case: 'Ilc$2015!'
Make it long and unique to this account

topics.rl: When you pay on an e-commerce site, the 'https://' and padlock mean the connection is encrypted, and your bank's OTP adds a second layer of authentication.

topics.h: India has a law for the online world and rules for the old phones in your drawer. Both protect citizens, one from crime and one from toxins.
p: The Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act), amended in 2008, gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, making e-commerce and e-governance legally valid.

It lays down provisions and penalties for cyber crimes such as hacking, identity theft and publishing obscene material online. Cyber cells in police departments investigate such crimes, and the Act provided for a Cyber Appellate Tribunal to hear appeals.
E-waste is discarded electrical and electronic equipment: old phones, computers, batteries, TVs, chargers. It contains harmful substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium.
Dumping or burning e-waste releases toxins into soil, water and air, harming the health of people (especially informal workers) and the environment.

Proper management: Reduce (buy only what you need, use devices longer), Reuse (repair, donate or resell working devices), Recycle (give e-waste to authorised collection centres or recyclers, not the regular garbage).

ex.q: Your family has an old laptop, a dead phone battery and a working but outdated tablet. What should you do with each?
st: Working tablet → reuse: donate it to a school or someone who needs it
Old laptop → wipe data, then sell back or give to an authorised e-waste recycler
Dead battery → drop at an authorised collection point; never throw it in household garbage or burn it
ex.a: Reuse what works; send the rest to authorised e-waste collection

topics.rl: India generates a large and growing amount of e-waste every year. Many brands now run take-back schemes, and authorised recyclers safely recover metals like copper and gold.

topics.t: Health, ergonomics and technology for everyone
topics.h: Hours of online classes and scrolling can leave you with dry eyes, a stiff neck and poor sleep. Technology should fit you, not the other way round.
p: Overuse of devices can cause eye strain (dry, tired eyes), poor posture and back or neck pain, repetitive stress injuries in wrists and fingers, sleep problems, and internet addiction.

Ergonomics is designing and arranging workspaces and devices to fit the user: screen at or slightly below eye level and about an arm's length away, back supported, feet flat on the floor, wrists straight.

Healthy habits: take regular breaks (e.g. the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds), keep screens away before bedtime, and clean devices and keyboards regularly.

Gender issues: girls are sometimes discouraged from computing; schools should give equal access and encouragement. Disability issues: students with disabilities need assistive technology such as screen readers, Braille keyboards, speech-to-text software and screen magnifiers.
Exam-style tasks: classify scenarios (plagiarism, hacking, phishing), compare copyright and patent, analyse etiquette, and recall IT Act provisions.

ex.q: Riya studies on her bed with her laptop on her lap for 3 hours. Suggest ergonomic fixes.
st: Use a table and chair with back support
Raise the screen to eye level (a stand or books)
Keep feet flat and wrists straight
Take a short break every 20–30 minutes and follow the 20-20-20 rule
ex.a: Proper desk setup plus regular breaks

topics.rl: Screen-reader software and Indian-language text-to-speech tools help visually impaired students study and appear in exams, while initiatives that bring more girls into coding are narrowing the gender gap in tech.

qa.q: Which part of the CPU decides whether 'marks >= 33' is True?
qa.e: Comparisons are logical operations, and logical operations are done by the ALU.

qa.q: Which part of the CPU fetches an instruction, decodes it and signals the other units?
qa.e: The CU manages and coordinates: it fetches, decodes and issues control signals. It does not compute results itself.

qa.q: Registers are best described as:
qa.a: Small, high-speed storage locations inside the CPU
qa.e: Registers sit inside the CPU and temporarily hold the data and instructions being processed. They are the fastest memory.

qa.q: Which statement correctly defines a computer?
qa.a: An electronic device that takes input, processes it under the control of instructions and gives output
qa.e: A computer is defined by input, processing under program control, and output. Arithmetic alone or storage alone is not enough.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The CPU is called the brain of the computer.
Reason (R): The CPU carries out instructions and controls the working of all other units.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The CPU executes instructions (via the ALU) and controls other units (via the CU), which is exactly why it is called the brain.

qa.q: In the block diagram, where are the program and data kept while the CPU is working on them?
qa.e: The CPU reads instructions and data from primary memory while processing. Input and output units only bring data in or send it out.

qa.q: Which pair of units together form the CPU's processing core along with registers?
qa.e: The CPU consists of the ALU, the CU and registers. RAM and hard disk are memory/storage outside the CPU.

qa.q: Case: A self-service railway ticket kiosk at a station reads your touch selection, computes the fare and prints the ticket. Which is the correct sequence of units used?
qa.e: Data first enters through an input device, is processed by the CPU, and the result is sent to an output device.

qa.q: Which of these is an output device?
qa.e: A projector displays processed data on a screen. The others send data into the computer.

qa.q: A doctor at AIIMS dictates notes into speech-to-text software. Which input device is used?
qa.e: A microphone captures sound and converts it to digital data, so it is an input device.

qa.q: Which device can work as both an input and an output device?
qa.e: A touch screen displays information and also senses your touch.

qa.q: Which one of the following is software, not hardware?
qa.e: An operating system is a set of programs. The others are physical components.

qa.q: What does a 3D printer produce?
qa.a: A solid three-dimensional object built layer by layer
qa.e: A 3D printer is an output device that builds physical objects from a digital design, layer upon layer.

qa.q: A shop uses a barcode reader at the billing counter. The barcode reader is:
qa.e: It reads the code on the product and sends it into the computer, which is input.

qa.q: Which statement about different computers is correct?
qa.a: Servers, laptops and smartphones all work on the input-process-output principle
qa.e: Every type of computer, from a server to a phone, takes input, processes it and produces output.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A speaker is an output device.
Reason (R): A speaker converts digital audio signals from the computer into sound.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A speaker turns processed digital data into sound for us, which is exactly what makes it an output device.

qa.q: Which technology defines second-generation computers?
qa.e: Transistors replaced vacuum tubes in the second generation, making computers smaller and more reliable.

qa.q: The stored-program concept, where both program and data are kept in memory, is credited to:
qa.e: Von Neumann's architecture keeps instructions and data together in memory. Modern computers still follow it.

qa.q: Who is known for designing the Analytical Engine, the first concept of a general-purpose programmable computer?
qa.e: Babbage's Analytical Engine (1834) had a mill and a store and could follow instructions on punched cards.

qa.q: Herman Hollerith's major contribution was:
qa.a: Using punched cards to tabulate census data
qa.e: Hollerith's tabulating machine read punched cards and processed the 1890 US census much faster.

qa.q: Which was mainly an adding machine built in 1642?
qa.e: Blaise Pascal built the Pascaline in 1642 to add and subtract mechanically.

qa.q: Fourth-generation computers are based on:
qa.e: Very Large Scale Integration put an entire CPU on one chip, the microprocessor, giving us personal computers.

qa.q: Smart watches and fitness bands that send data to a phone are examples of:
qa.a: Wearable devices, part of the IoT trend
qa.e: Wearables are small computers worn on the body, and when connected they are part of the Internet of Things.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): First-generation computers were very large and produced a lot of heat.
Reason (R): They used thousands of vacuum tubes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Vacuum tubes were bulky and hot, so machines using thousands of them were huge and heat-producing.

qa.q: How many megabytes are there in 4 GB?
A file is 8192 bytes. What is its size in KB?
qa.e: Divide by 1024 to go from bytes to KB: 8192 ÷ 1024 = 8 KB.

qa.q: How many bits are there in 3 bytes?
qa.e: 1 byte = 8 bits, so 3 bytes = 24 bits.

qa.q: How many nibbles make 1 KB?
qa.e: 1 KB = 1024 bytes and each byte has 2 nibbles, so 1024 × 2 = 2048 nibbles.

qa.q: Which is the correct ascending order of memory units?
qa.a: Byte < KB < MB < GB < TB < PB
qa.e: Each unit is 1024 times the previous: byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB.

qa.q: A phone has 128 GB storage. How many such phones together hold 1 TB?
Why does a computer need memory at all?
qa.a: To hold the data, instructions and results the CPU works with
qa.e: The CPU can only process what is in memory: the instructions to follow and the data to work on.

qa.q: How many bytes are there in 2 MB?
Which memory loses its contents when the power is switched off?
qa.e: RAM is volatile, so it needs power to keep data.

qa.q: Where are the instructions needed to start up (boot) a computer usually stored?
qa.e: ROM is non-volatile, so boot instructions remain available every time the computer is switched on.

qa.q: Cache memory is placed between:
qa.e: Cache is a small, fast buffer between the CPU and main memory that holds frequently used data.

qa.q: Compared with primary memory, secondary memory is:
qa.e: Secondary storage trades speed for large, cheap, permanent capacity.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a secondary storage device?
qa.e: RAM is primary memory. SSDs, memory cards and DVDs store data permanently as secondary storage.

qa.q: Arrange from fastest to slowest: RAM, registers, hard disk, cache.
qa.e: Registers are inside the CPU and fastest, then cache, then RAM, and the hard disk is slowest.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The CPU keeps frequently used data in cache memory.
Reason (R): Cache is faster than RAM.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because cache is faster than RAM, keeping frequently used data there reduces the time the CPU waits.

qa.q: A student says, 'ROM is read-only, so it is volatile.' What is wrong?
qa.a: ROM is non-volatile: it keeps data without power
qa.e: 'Read-only' is about not writing normally; 'volatile' is about losing data without power. ROM keeps its data.

qa.q: Which bus is bidirectional?
qa.e: Data must travel both from memory to the CPU (read) and from the CPU to memory (write).

qa.q: When the CPU wants to read memory location 2048, the number 2048 travels on the:
qa.e: The location number is an address, so it goes on the address bus. The value stored there comes back on the data bus.

qa.q: How many memory locations can a CPU address with 16 address lines?
qa.e: Each extra line doubles the count: 2¹⁶ = 65536 locations.

qa.q: Which device is most likely to use a microcontroller rather than a full general-purpose computer?
qa.e: A washing machine runs one fixed set of tasks, so a small, cheap microcontroller is ideal.

qa.q: The clock speed of a microprocessor is measured in:
qa.e: Clock speed counts cycles per second, which is measured in hertz.

qa.q: A processor with a word size of 64 bits can:
qa.a: Process 64 bits of data at a time
qa.e: Word size is the amount of data the processor handles in one operation.

qa.q: What is a microprocessor?
qa.a: A CPU built on a single integrated-circuit chip
qa.e: The microprocessor puts the entire CPU on one chip, a key 4th-generation development.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The address bus is unidirectional.
Reason (R): The data bus carries data both to and from the CPU.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but the direction of the data bus does not explain why the address bus is one-way; that is because only the CPU sends addresses.

qa.q: Which of these is information rather than raw data?
qa.e: The average is the result of processing raw marks, so it is meaningful information.

qa.q: An XML file storing book details with tags like <title> is an example of:
qa.e: Tags give some organisation, but it is not a strict table, so it is semi-structured.

qa.q: Instagram reels and photos are mostly:
qa.e: Images and videos do not follow a fixed row-column format.

qa.q: Which data type is the easiest to search with simple queries like 'all students with marks > 90'?
qa.e: Structured data is in fixed fields, so it can be filtered directly.

qa.q: When you delete a file on Windows, where does it usually go first?
qa.e: Normal deletion just moves the file to the Recycle Bin, so it can be restored.

qa.q: Before selling an old phone, why should you do a secure wipe rather than just delete files?
qa.a: Deleted data can often be recovered by recovery tools
qa.e: Plain deletion often leaves data on the storage until overwritten, so a buyer could recover it.

qa.q: Which step comes immediately after data capturing?
qa.e: Captured data is first stored so that it can later be retrieved and processed.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Data and information mean the same thing.
Reason (R): Information is obtained by processing data.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: Data is raw; information is processed data. So A is false while R is true.

qa.q: Which language is directly understood by the CPU without translation?
qa.e: Machine language is written in binary, the only form the CPU executes directly.

qa.q: Which translator converts assembly-language mnemonics into machine code?
qa.e: Assembly code is converted by an assembler.

qa.q: Which statement about an interpreter is correct?
qa.a: It translates and executes one statement at a time, stopping at the first error
qa.e: An interpreter processes line by line, so it stops as soon as it meets an error.

qa.q: A student installs a new webcam and the computer cannot use it until certain software is installed. That software is a:
qa.e: A device driver lets the OS communicate with a specific hardware device.

qa.q: Which of these is a system utility?
qa.e: Utilities maintain the computer, e.g. antivirus, backup, disk cleanup.

qa.q: Python is called a high-level language because:
qa.a: Its statements are close to human language and independent of the hardware
qa.e: High-level languages use English-like words and are portable across machines; they still need translation.

qa.q: Which is an example of an IDE used for Python?
qa.e: IDLE is Python's Integrated Development and Learning Environment, combining an editor and an interpreter shell.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A compiled program usually runs faster than the same program interpreted line by line.
Reason (R): A compiler translates the entire program into machine code once, before execution.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since translation is done once in advance, execution does not pause to translate each line.

qa.q: A spreadsheet such as MS Excel is an example of:
qa.e: Spreadsheets are ready-made for many users and many tasks, so they are general-purpose applications.

qa.q: Software developed only for the fee collection of a particular school is:
qa.e: It is tailored for one organisation's specific needs.

qa.q: Which is free and open source software?
qa.e: LibreOffice's source code is open for anyone to study, modify and share.

qa.q: What is the key difference between freeware and open source software?
qa.a: Freeware is free to use but its source code is closed; open source shares the source code
qa.e: Both can be free of cost, but only open source gives access to the source code.

qa.q: Proprietary software means:
qa.a: The owner keeps the source code closed and users need a licence
qa.e: Proprietary software is owned by a company that controls how it is used and keeps the code private.

qa.q: A web browser is classified as:
qa.e: It helps the user perform a task (browsing), so it is application software.

qa.q: Which of these is customised software?
qa.e: The reservation system was designed for the specific needs of Indian Railways.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Python is free and open source.
Reason (R): Its source code is publicly available and can be modified and redistributed.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Public, modifiable source code is the defining feature of open source, which explains A.

qa.q: The operating system mainly acts as:
qa.a: An interface between the user and the hardware, managing resources
qa.e: The OS hides hardware details from the user and manages CPU, memory, files and devices.

qa.q: Which OS function decides which running program gets the CPU next?
qa.e: Scheduling programs on the CPU is process management.

qa.q: Allocating RAM to a newly opened app and freeing it when the app closes is:
qa.e: Handling primary memory space is the job of memory management.

qa.q: A Linux user types 'ls' to list files. Which type of interface is this?
qa.e: Typing text commands is a command-based (command-line) interface.

qa.q: Which is NOT an operating system?
qa.e: MS Word is an application (word processor); the others are operating systems.

qa.q: Creating folders, naming files and controlling who may open them is part of:
qa.e: The OS's file system organises and protects files and folders.

qa.q: Which statement is correct?
qa.a: RAM is volatile, ROM is non-volatile; a compiler translates the whole program, an interpreter one line at a time
qa.e: This pairs the correct property with each memory and each translator.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A user can work on a computer without knowing how its hardware works.
Reason (R): The operating system provides an interface that hides hardware details.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the OS hides the hardware behind a friendly interface, users don't need hardware knowledge.

qa.q: How many characters can ASCII represent?
qa.e: ASCII is a 7-bit code, and 2⁷ = 128.

qa.q: What is the ASCII code of 'C'?
What is the ASCII code of 'd'?
Which statement best describes encoding?
qa.a: Representing each character by a unique code that can be stored in binary
qa.e: Encoding maps characters to standard codes; it is not about secrecy or compression.

qa.q: The digit character '7' typed on a keyboard has ASCII code:
qa.e: Digit characters start at '0' = 48, so '7' = 48 + 7 = 55.

qa.q: A character has ASCII code 72. Which character is it?
qa.e: 72 − 65 = 7, so it is 7 letters after 'A', which is 'H'.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Encoding and encryption are the same.
Reason (R): Encryption converts data into a secret form using a key.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: Encryption hides data with a key; encoding just represents it. So A is false and R is true.

qa.q: What is the difference between the ASCII codes of 'M' and 'm'?
qa.e: Every lower-case letter is 32 more than its upper-case partner (e.g. 77 and 109).

qa.q: How many characters can ISCII represent?
qa.e: ISCII is an 8-bit code, and 2⁸ = 256.

qa.q: Which is the 7-bit ASCII binary code for 'A'?
What is the 7-bit ASCII code for 'T' (decimal 84)?
qa.e: 84 = 64 + 16 + 4, so the bits for 64, 16 and 4 are 1: 1010100.

qa.q: Why was ISCII developed?
qa.a: To represent Indian language scripts, which ASCII cannot
qa.e: ASCII's 128 codes have no room for Indian scripts, so ISCII added them using 8 bits.

qa.q: The sum of the ASCII codes of the letters in 'CAB' is:
Which statement about ISCII is correct?
qa.a: Its first 128 codes match ASCII and Indian aksharas are in the upper range
qa.e: ISCII extends ASCII to 8 bits, keeping ASCII's 128 codes and placing aksharas in 160–255.

qa.q: ASCII code 97 decodes to:
qa.e: 97 is the code for lower-case 'a'.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): ASCII cannot store a Tamil word.
Reason (R): ASCII has only 128 codes, used for English letters, digits, symbols and control characters.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: With all 128 codes used up by English characters and controls, there is no room for Tamil script.

qa.q: Which Unicode encoding uses a fixed 4 bytes for every character?
qa.e: UTF-32 stores each character in exactly 32 bits = 4 bytes.

qa.q: How many bytes does the 6-letter word 'PYTHON' need in UTF-32?
qa.e: Each character takes 4 bytes in UTF-32: 6 × 4 = 24.

qa.q: Why is Unicode called a superset of ASCII?
qa.a: Its first 128 code points are the same as the ASCII codes
qa.e: Every ASCII character keeps the same number in Unicode, so ASCII text is valid Unicode.

qa.q: The Unicode value of 'क' is U+0915. In which number system is 0915 written?
qa.e: Unicode code points are written in hexadecimal after 'U+'.

qa.q: What is the main advantage of Unicode over ASCII and ISCII?
qa.a: It gives a unique code to characters of almost all world scripts
qa.e: Unicode is universal, covering nearly all scripts and symbols in one standard.

qa.q: A UTF-8 file contains only English letters. How many bytes does each character use?
qa.e: UTF-8 encodes ASCII characters in a single byte, so English text stays compact.

qa.q: The Devanagari block in Unicode starts at:
qa.e: Devanagari characters occupy U+0900 to U+097F.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): UTF-32 files are usually larger than UTF-8 files for English text.
Reason (R): UTF-32 uses 4 bytes for every character, while UTF-8 uses 1 byte for English letters.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Four bytes versus one byte per English letter makes UTF-32 files about four times larger, explaining A.

qa.q: What is the radix of the binary number system?
qa.e: Binary uses two symbols, 0 and 1, so its base is 2.

qa.q: Convert (10110)₂ to decimal.
What is the decimal value of (70)₈?
Why do computers use the binary system?
qa.a: Electronic components such as transistors have two stable states, ON and OFF
qa.e: Two states map neatly to 1 and 0, making circuits simple and reliable.

qa.q: In (4352)₁₀, what is the place value of 3?
qa.e: 3 is in the hundreds place (10²), so its value is 300.

qa.q: Which of these digit strings can NOT be a binary number?
qa.e: Binary allows only 0 and 1; the digit 2 is not allowed.

qa.q: What is the decimal value of the largest 5-bit binary number?
qa.e: The largest 5-bit number is 11111 = 2⁵ − 1 = 31.

qa.q: In positional expansion, what power of 10 does the digit 5 in (237.5)₁₀ get?
qa.e: The first digit to the right of the decimal point has position −1.

qa.q: Which digits does the octal system use?
qa.e: Base 8 has eight symbols, 0 through 7.

qa.q: How many bits does one hexadecimal digit represent?
qa.e: 16 = 2⁴, so each hex digit maps to exactly 4 bits.

qa.q: What is the decimal value of the hex digit D?
The 24-bit RGB colour code for pure blue is:
qa.e: In RGB order, blue is the last two hex digits, so only they are FF.

qa.q: What is the decimal value of one colour channel 'FF'?
qa.e: FF = 15 × 16 + 15 = 255, the maximum for 8 bits.

qa.q: Why are memory addresses usually written in hexadecimal?
qa.a: Hex is a compact way to write long binary numbers
qa.e: Each hex digit replaces 4 bits, making addresses short and readable. Computers still store binary.

qa.q: Which of these is a valid octal number?
qa.e: Octal digits must be 0–7. 8, 9 and A are not allowed.

qa.q: A colour code is 00FF00. What colour is it?
qa.e: Only the middle (green) channel is at maximum.

qa.q: Convert (25)₁₀ to binary.
qa.e: 25 → remainders 1, 0, 0, 1, 1 read bottom-up give 11001 (16 + 8 + 1 = 25).

qa.q: Convert (100)₁₀ to octal.
Convert (47)₁₀ to hexadecimal.
qa.e: 47 ÷ 16 = 2 r 15 (F), 2 ÷ 16 = 0 r 2; bottom-up gives 2F.

qa.q: Convert (200)₁₀ to hexadecimal.
When converting decimal to binary by repeated division, the remainders are read:
qa.a: From the last remainder to the first
qa.e: The last remainder is the most significant bit, so read bottom-up.

qa.q: How many bits are in the binary form of (64)₁₀?
qa.e: 64 = 2⁶ = 1000000, which has 7 bits.

qa.q: Convert (19)₁₀ to binary.
qa.e: 19 = 16 + 2 + 1, so the bits for 16, 2 and 1 are set: 10011.

qa.q: Convert (83)₁₀ to octal.
Convert (110101)₂ to decimal.
Convert (725)₈ to decimal.
Convert (2B)₁₆ to decimal.
Convert (3A7)₁₆ to decimal.
Convert (1000000)₂ to decimal.
qa.e: A 1 followed by six 0s is 2⁶ = 64.

qa.q: What is the decimal value of (777)₈?
Which of these has the largest value?
Convert (FF)₁₆ to decimal.
Convert (101110)₂ to octal.
qa.e: Groups of 3 from the right: 101 | 110 → 5 and 6, so 56.

qa.q: Convert (11010110)₂ to hexadecimal.
Convert (47)₈ to binary.
Convert (A3)₁₆ to binary.
Convert (27)₈ to hexadecimal.

qa.a: For inputs 1 and 1, OR gives 1 but XOR gives 0

qa.q: What is the FIRST step in solving a problem with a computer?
qa.e: You must understand inputs, outputs and requirements before planning or coding.

qa.q: While analysing 'find the average of three numbers', what are the inputs?

qa.q: Why should an algorithm be developed before coding?
qa.a: It gives a clear plan, so errors in logic are found early

qa.q: Which sequence of problem-solving steps is correct?
qa.a: Analyse → algorithm → code → test and debug
qa.e: Understand the problem, plan it, write it, then check it.

qa.q: A computer can solve a problem only when:
qa.a: It is given precise, step-by-step instructions
qa.e: Computers follow instructions exactly; they cannot fill gaps in vague instructions.

qa.q: For a program that converts temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit, what is the output?

qa.e: This is analysis: clarify requirements, inputs and outputs before designing a solution.

qa.q: What is source code?
qa.a: A program written in a high-level language by a programmer
qa.e: Source code is human-written code, which a compiler or interpreter translates to machine code.

qa.e: Errors are called bugs; removing them is debugging.

qa.e: Acceptance testing is done by, or for, the user to accept the product.

qa.a: To make the logic clear and catch mistakes before coding

qa.e: The same input always leads to the same result at each step, with no guessing.

qa.q:

Reason (R): An algorithm describes the logic of a solution in plain steps, not in a particular language's syntax.

qa.e: Personal details in public posts become part of a lasting footprint and can be misused.

qa.q: Where are digital footprints stored?
qa.a: On your device (e.g. browser history, cookies) and on websites' servers
qa.e: Browsers store history and cookies locally, while sites keep logs and data on their servers.

qa.q: Which practice reduces your digital footprint?
qa.a: Reviewing app permissions and limiting public posts of personal information
qa.e: Limiting what apps can collect and what you share publicly shrinks your footprint.

qa.q: Which statement best describes the impact of digital technology on society?
qa.a: It makes many tasks faster and easier, but it can also be misused, so it must be used responsibly
qa.e: Digital technology speeds up banking, learning and communication, yet the same tools can be misused for fraud or harassment. That is why responsible use matters.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): We should think before posting anything online.
Reason (R): Our digital footprint is long-lasting and can be seen by others in the future.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because posts last and can be viewed later, thinking first protects our reputation.

qa.q: Who is a netizen?
qa.a: A person who uses the internet
qa.e: Netizen comes from 'internet' and 'citizen'.

qa.q: 'Don't feed the troll' means:
qa.a: Do not respond to people who post provocative comments to upset others
qa.e: Trolls want attention; ignoring them takes away their fuel.

qa.q: Which is an example of being ethical online?
qa.a: Asking permission before using someone's photograph
qa.e: Respecting creators' rights is ethical behaviour.

qa.q: 'Be precise' in communication etiquette mainly means:
qa.a: Respect others' time and data by keeping messages and attachments to what is needed
qa.e: Short, clear messages and sensible file sizes respect the receiver's time and data limits.

qa.q: Which social media habit shows 'be secure'?
qa.a: Using a strong, unique password and not accepting unknown friend requests
qa.e: Security means protecting your account and knowing who you connect with.

qa.q: Case: Arjun receives a message saying a famous actor has died, with no source. What should he do?
qa.a: Check credible news sources before forwarding, or not forward at all
qa.e: Verifying before sharing stops the spread of fake news.

qa.q: Typing a message entirely in CAPITAL LETTERS is considered:
qa.a: Rude, because it is read as shouting
qa.e: Online, all caps signals shouting, which breaks politeness etiquette.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Before uploading a group photo, we should take our friends' consent.
Reason (R): A person can never delete a photo after uploading it.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true because consent respects others' privacy. R is false: the uploader can delete their own post, though copies may already have spread.

qa.q: Which IPR protects a new invention, such as a new type of water filter?
qa.e: Inventions are protected by patents, usually for about 20 years.

qa.q: Which IPR protects the code of a computer program?
qa.e: Software code is treated as a literary work and is protected by copyright.

qa.q: Presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own without giving credit is:
qa.e: Plagiarism is passing off another's work as your own.

qa.q: A logo, brand name or symbol that identifies a company's products is protected by a:
qa.e: Trademarks protect brand identity.

qa.q: Which licence is commonly used to share creative works like photos and music with conditions such as giving credit?
qa.e: Creative Commons licences are designed for creative content.

qa.q: Which of these helps protect sensitive personal data?
qa.e: Encryption scrambles data and authentication controls who can access it.

qa.q: Installing a paid software copied from a friend without a licence is:
qa.e: Using or distributing software without a valid licence is piracy.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Software released under the GNU GPL can be modified and shared.
Reason (R): The GPL is a free software licence that gives users the freedom to use, study, modify and distribute the code.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The freedoms granted by the GPL are exactly why modifying and sharing is allowed.

qa.q: What is cyber crime?
qa.a: A crime in which a computer or network is used as a tool or a target
qa.e: Using computers to commit crimes, or attacking computers themselves, is cyber crime.

qa.q: An email that appears to come from your bank asks you to 'verify' your password by clicking a link. This is:
qa.e: Fake messages designed to steal credentials are phishing.

qa.q: Ransomware attacks usually:
qa.a: Encrypt the victim's data and demand payment to unlock it
qa.e: Ransomware holds data hostage by encrypting it.

qa.q: A white hat hacker is someone who:
qa.a: Is authorised to find and report security weaknesses
qa.e: Ethical hackers work with permission to improve security.

qa.q: Someone uses a stolen Aadhaar number and photo to take a loan in another person's name. This is:
qa.e: Misusing someone's identity for money is financial identity theft.

qa.q: Repeatedly sending threatening messages to a classmate on social media is:
qa.e: Harassing someone through digital media is cyberbullying, and it should be reported.

qa.q: An email shows 'From: principal@school.edu.in' but was actually sent by a stranger. This trick is called:
qa.e: Spoofing forges the sender's address to make a message look trustworthy.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): One should never share an OTP, even with someone claiming to be from the bank.
Reason (R): Banks never ask customers for their OTP, and an OTP lets the holder authorise transactions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since an OTP authorises transactions and banks never ask for it, sharing it is always risky.

qa.q: Which malware disguises itself as useful software?
qa.e: Like the Trojan horse of legend, it hides harm inside something that looks useful.

qa.q: Which malware spreads across networks by copying itself, without needing to attach to a file?
qa.e: A worm self-replicates over networks; a virus needs a host file.

qa.q: Which is the best defence against losing data to ransomware?
qa.e: With a backup you can restore files without paying.

qa.q: Why should you look for 'https://' before entering card details?
qa.a: It shows the connection to the site is encrypted
qa.e: HTTPS encrypts data between your browser and the site.

qa.q: Software that shows a flood of unwanted pop-up ads is:
qa.e: Adware displays unwanted advertising.

qa.q: A digital signature is used to:
qa.a: Verify the sender's identity and that the document has not been changed
qa.e: Digital signatures provide authenticity and integrity.

qa.q: Case: Meena lost ₹5,000 through a fake UPI request. What should she do first?
qa.a: Report it immediately on helpline 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in and inform her bank
qa.e: Quick reporting to the cyber helpline and bank gives the best chance of stopping the money.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Keeping the operating system updated helps prevent cyber attacks.
Reason (R): Updates often fix security weaknesses that attackers could exploit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Patching known weaknesses closes doors attackers use.

qa.q: The Information Technology Act of India was enacted in:
qa.e: The IT Act was passed in 2000 and amended in 2008.

qa.q: Which is a key purpose of the IT Act, 2000?
qa.a: To give legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures
qa.e: It made e-transactions and e-documents legally valid and addressed cyber crimes.

qa.q: Where can a victim of cyber crime file a complaint?
qa.a: The cyber cell of the police or the national cyber crime portal
qa.e: Cyber cells and the official portal handle cyber crime complaints.

qa.q: What is e-waste?
qa.e: E-waste refers to physical electronic devices that are thrown away.

qa.q: Why is dumping e-waste in landfills harmful?
qa.a: Toxic substances like lead and mercury can leak into soil and water
qa.e: Heavy metals contaminate the environment and harm health.

qa.q: Donating your old but working phone to a needy student is an example of:
qa.e: The device continues to be used as it is, which is reuse.

qa.q: The IT Act was amended in which year to address newer cyber crimes?
qa.e: The major amendment came in 2008.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): E-waste should be handed over to authorised recyclers.
Reason (R): Authorised recyclers can safely recover useful materials and handle toxic components without harming people or the environment.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Safe recovery and handling is exactly why authorised recycling is recommended.

qa.q: Ergonomics is the study of:
qa.a: Designing workplaces and devices to fit the user comfortably and safely
qa.e: Ergonomics aims to reduce strain and injury by fitting tools to people.

qa.q: Which practice reduces eye strain?
qa.e: Regular distant focusing gives the eye muscles a rest.

qa.q: Pain in the wrists from long hours of typing and mouse use is an example of:
qa.e: Repeating the same motions for long periods strains muscles and tendons.

qa.q: Which is the correct position for a monitor?
qa.a: At or slightly below eye level, about an arm's length away
qa.e: This keeps the neck neutral and reduces eye strain.

qa.q: A screen reader helps:
qa.a: Visually impaired users by reading out the text on the screen
qa.e: Screen readers convert on-screen text to speech or Braille.

qa.q: Which step promotes gender equality in a school computer lab?
qa.a: Giving girls and boys equal access, time and encouragement to use computers
qa.e: Equal access and encouragement address the gender gap in computing.

qa.q: Case: A student copies code from a website into a project without credit, and another breaks into the school server. Classify the two acts.
qa.e: Using someone's code as your own is plagiarism; unauthorised access to a server is hacking.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Using a phone in bed late at night can disturb sleep.
Reason (R): Screen use before bedtime keeps the brain alert and delays sleep.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Late screen use stimulates the brain and pushes sleep later, explaining A.
